newsitem.title: FRANCE: French museums head denies guilt on looted art.
newsitem.headline: French museums head denies guilt on looted art.

text.p: The head of the French museums network protested on Tuesday against accusations that it had intentionally dragged its feet in trying to identify owners of nearly 2,000 works of art thought seized from Jews during World War Two.

"We have been wronged because these works of art were always traceable. We may not have published a special catalogue of them but they have been included in inventories since the 1950s," said Francoise Cachin.

She recalled that of 60,000 works of art recovered by France from the Nazis after the war, 45,000 were returned to their rightful owners or heirs, 15,000 which were of little value were sold and only 2,000 remained under "provisional administration."

The accusations against the museums by the Cour des Comptes auditing board followed a weekend announcement by Prime Minister Alain Juppe that he would create a commission to probe the scope of seizures by the Nazis and their Vichy French collaborators from 1940 to 1944.
There have been increasing calls for the government to clarify the status of property never returned to their rightful owners after the war.
The works of art have drawn special attention because they included priceless items by Gauguin, Renoir and Rodin.

Cachin told French television that she believed most of the 2,000 remaining paintings and sculptures, which are on show in museums around the country, were never claimed "because they were not stolen during the occupation but sold.
"It's a sorry thing to say but the art market was never as active as it was during the occupation," she said.
Cachin said she believed many of the works were sold by art dealers to German officers and were not claimed later by the dealers for fear of being accused of collaboration.

Serge Cwajgenbaum, president of the Paris-based European Jewish Congress, challenged Cachin's version saying many works were acquired at rock-bottom prices by shady dealers from Jews virtually forced to sell their goods.
Nazi hunter Arno Klarsfeld also dismissed Cachin's version saying the museums "did absolutely nothing in the immediate post-war years to identify the owners of the art works."

Henri Hajdenberg, president of the Council of French Jewish Institutions (CRIF), said: "Maybe some families will discover that they are heirs to this or that family sent to death camps but such cases will probably be few in number.
"What the French Jewish community wants is that the truth be established, that is all," he told French television.
The controversy came amid moves to shed light on the dark years of World War Two in other countries including neutral Switzerland and Sweden.
Some 76,000 of the 320,000 Jews in France at the time were sent to Nazi concentration camps, including 11,000 children. Only about 2,800 of those who were deported survived.

Although the art works have drawn special attention, other issues the Juppe commission is to probe include the fate of flats seized from Jews sent to death camps and which the Paris city council "inherited" from the retreating Nazis.
